Pleasure? I mean... no. No, not really. It's like I was saying before, about the restaurant and everything just feeling gray. It’s like that with everything now. 

I used to love working on my car, right? I have this older Honda, and I used to spend hours out in the driveway on my days off. Harming myself? Um... I mean, I wouldn't say I have a plan or anything. I'm not sitting around figuring out how to do it. But... yeah, the thought of just not being here anymore... it crosses my mind. 

It usually happens when I'm lying in bed, you know? Like, before an early shift. Sometimes I have to be at the restaurant by 6:00 AM to help set up for the breakfast rush. We have to wipe down all the tables, fill all the salt and pepper shakers—which is this incredibly tedious process because the salt always clumps up if you don't put those little grains of rice in there—and make sure the coffee stations are completely stocked with the right creamers and those little pink and yellow sugar packets. And I'll be lying there in the dark, maybe around 4:30 in the morning, looking at the glowing red numbers on my alarm clock, just dreading having to get up and put on the uniform. My uniform is this awful stiff black button-down shirt that always feels tight across the shoulders, and these black slacks that collect every piece of lint in a ten-mile radius. 

And while I'm lying there, staring at the clock, feeling that heavy weight in my chest, I just think... it would be so much easier if I just didn't wake up. If the alarm went off and I just wasn't there to hear it. It's not that I want to violently end things, it's just this overwhelming feeling of exhaustion. Like, if I just slipped away in my sleep, I wouldn't have to keep trying so hard. Family and friends? I mean... it's like I was saying about the movie nights. It's just... I don't feel that connection anymore. I used to be pretty social, you know? Before this? No, no... I mean, sure, everyone gets down sometimes, right? Like back when I was taking a couple of classes at the community college, I failed a business math midterm. I was pretty bummed out for a few days, mostly because I had spent all this money on this fancy graphing calculator, a TI-84, the silver edition with the slide-off cover, and I still bombed the test. The old ones were this classic diner-style cream color with a thick rim, and they held the heat really well. The new ones are stark white and they chip if you even look at them wrong. I remember standing back by the dish pit, unboxing the new mugs—they came in these huge cardboard boxes packed with that really annoying styrofoam that breaks into tiny little static-cling balls that stick to your black uniform pants no matter how much you brush at them—and just feeling this sudden, crushing weight of guilt and sadness. Just out of nowhere. I kept thinking about how I was failing my wife, how I'd never be able to afford a better house for my daughter, just all of it hitting me at once while I was pulling these cheap mugs out of the box. It’s just this cycle I can’t get out of, where every little thing just points back to me being a failure.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's been a while now. I mean, looking back, I think there have been times, yeah. Not exactly like this, maybe not as tied to the mortgage, but... but definitely times where things felt just... off. It's just everything else that feels so different and so heavy.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Pleasure? I mean... no. No, not really. We used to have family movie night every Friday. We'd make popcorn on the stove—not the microwave kind, but the real kind with oil and salt—and pick something to watch. I used to love sitting there on the couch with them, laughing at some silly comedy. But now, I just sit there staring at the screen. The popcorn tastes like nothing, and I don't even crack a smile when my daughter laughs at the jokes. I'm just physically in the room, but my mind is just... blank. Or it's stuck on how I'm ruining everything for them. So, no, the things I used to enjoy, they just don't do anything for me anymore. It's all just... flat.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead during these last 14 months?\n\nPatient: Harming myself? Um... I mean, I wouldn't say I have a plan or anything. I'm not sitting around figuring out how to do it. Sometimes I have to be at the restaurant by 6:00 AM to help set up for the breakfast rush. If the alarm went off and I just wasn't there to hear it. It's not that I want to violently end things, it's just this overwhelming feeling of exhaustion. Like, if I just slipped away in my sleep, I wouldn't have to keep trying so hard. Changes in my appetite? Yeah, it's... it's been really weird, honestly. My eating has just been completely all over the place. There's no consistency to it anymore. 

Like, at the restaurant, we get a free shift meal if we work a double, or half off if it's just a regular shift. I used to always look forward to it. I'd usually get the patty melt—it comes on this thick marbled rye bread that the line cooks toast perfectly on the flat top grill, with those deeply caramelized onions and gooey Swiss cheese. But for a lot of these past 14 months, there are whole weeks where I'll ring in my staff meal, and when they finally put it up in the pass-through window under those long red heat lamps that make all the food look kind of orange, I just stare at it. I barely touch it. I'll take the little red plastic basket back to the break area, maybe eat a single fry or just push the sandwich around on the wax paper, but my stomach just feels totally tied in knots. I usually end up just scraping the whole thing into the trash before I clock out. 

But then, on the flip side, there are other nights where the complete opposite happens. I'll get home from a closing shift, my feet are absolutely throbbing from standing on those thick rubber anti-fatigue mats all night—which, by the way, do not actually stop your fatigue at all—and I'll walk into my house. The kitchen will be pitch black except for the little glowing green numbers on the microwave clock, and I won't even bother flipping on the overhead switch. I'll just open the refrigerator door and let that one harsh little bulb light up the room, and I'll just stand there in my work uniform and eat whatever is in the kitchen. 

I'll eat cold leftover macaroni and cheese straight out of the plastic Tupperware container, or just grab handfuls of shredded cheddar cheese out of the bag, or I'll go into the pantry and eat half a sleeve of slightly stale saltine crackers over the sink so I don't drop crumbs. And the thing is, I'm not even really hungry when I do it. I'm just eating to try and feel settled, you know? Like maybe if I just stuff enough random food into my stomach, it'll somehow push down all that heavy, guilty garbage in my chest so I can finally get an hour of peace. So, yeah, it just bounces back and forth between those two extremes.

Voices? Um... yeah. I mean, it’s really hard to talk about because it makes me sound, well, you know. But yeah, I have. 

It usually happens when things get really quiet and I'm by myself. Like, when I’m closing the restaurant. It’ll just say my name. Or it’ll whisper, really clearly, that I’m going to lose everything. My family, my life, just... everything. And it sounds so incredibly real, Doctor. It doesn't feel like a thought bouncing around inside my own brain. It sounds like a physical person standing just over my left shoulder, right behind the collar of my uniform shirt. I’ll literally drop the broom I'm holding and spin around to check, completely expecting to see my manager or maybe one of the busboys who forgot his keys standing there messing with me. But there's never anyone there. It’s just me and the hum of the ice machine in the back.

And it’s not just at the restaurant, either. It happens when I’m sitting alone in the condo, too. Sometimes after my wife and daughter have gone to bed, I’ll just stay out in the living room. The TV will be off, and the only light is whatever is bleeding through the horizontal blinds from the parking lot, making these long striped shadows across the carpet. I’ll just be sitting there on that brown recliner I was telling you about, completely still, and I’ll hear it again. That same low whisper. I always turn around to look toward the hallway. I'll just whip my head around, my heart absolutely hammering against my ribs, because it sounds so real I’m convinced someone broke in and is standing right there in the dark behind my chair. But... it's just empty space. So, yeah, I have been hearing that.

Harm myself? Oh, no. No, I don't... I don't have a plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting around trying to figure out how to do something to myself. It’s not like that.
